calculs.t0.diurnalReg.con2: Method assumes proportionality between sap flow and ETo that may not hold under water stress
calculs.t0.diurnalReg.how: Alternative method to estimate ΔT0ax without assuming zero sap flow at night. Variable transformation: Y = 1/T600 and X = ETo^(1/β). Robust linear regression (Theil-Sen) between X and Y. The intercept gives 1/T600_max. Uses only diurnal data (6h–20h) to avoid nighttime sap flow bias.
calculs.t0.diurnalReg.label: Diurnal regression
calculs.t0.diurnalReg.pro1: Does not assume zero nighttime flow — more robust when nighttime transpiration occurs
calculs.t0.diurnalReg.pro2: Uses diurnal data (more abundant) and robust regression down-weights outliers
calculs.t0.diurnalReg.title: Diurnal regression — Regaldo & Ritter 2007
calculs.t0.doubleReg.con1: Needs enough upper points (>= 3) for a night — otherwise falls back to max
calculs.t0.doubleReg.con2: Less suited when residual nocturnal transpiration is very uniform (low variance)
calculs.t0.doubleReg.how: For each night: (1) linear regression on every nocturnal ΔT (captures the average trend — sensor drift, cooling), (2) keep only the points above this line (the upper envelope, close to ΔT0ax), (3) regress again on the filtered set. T0 = mean of the kept points. More robust than a plain max — a single spike won't bias the result.
calculs.t0.doubleReg.label: Double regression
calculs.t0.doubleReg.pro2: Adapts to gradual thermal drift over the night
calculs.t0.doubleReg.title: Double regression — upper-points filter
calculs.t0.envData.con1: Requires a synchronized env file (VPD + PAR or Rg) — ≤ 30-min granularity recommended
calculs.t0.envData.con2: Sensitive to column units: VPD in hPa with kPa threshold = no match (the per-slider range hints flag this)
calculs.t0.envData.how: Keeps only rows where ALL no-flow conditions hold simultaneously: VPD < threshold AND (PAR < threshold and/or Rg < threshold) AND nocturnal clock window AND thermal stability (CV of ΔT below threshold over an intra-night rolling window). PAR and Rg can both be selected — the algorithm ANDs the filters. For each valid night, T0 = mean ΔT over the most stable window. Nights without a valid window are linearly interpolated from neighbors (TRACC).
calculs.t0.envData.label: Env. data
calculs.t0.envData.pro1: Physically grounded: looks for actual no-flow periods rather than assuming night is calm
calculs.t0.envData.pro2: Works in biomes where Nocturnal max fails (Sahel, humid tropics — non-zero nighttime VPD)
calculs.t0.envData.ref: Oishi et al. 2008/2016; Rabbel 2016; Ward 2017; Wang 2025
calculs.t0.envData.title: Env. data (VpdPar — Oishi 2008/2016)
calculs.t0.movingWindow.con1: Lag in detecting rapid changes (sudden drought)
calculs.t0.movingWindow.con2: Choice of N days (default 7) is arbitrary — try 5–10 depending on context
calculs.t0.movingWindow.desc: Nocturnal max over an N-day rolling window
calculs.t0.movingWindow.how: For each day D: (1) max ΔT over the nocturnal window (e.g. 20h–6h) → night_max(D). (2) T0(D) = max{ night_max(D−n) … night_max(D+n) } over an N-day rolling window centred on D (default 7 days, Lu 2004). This two-step approach smooths slow sensor drift (aging, trunk growth) without masking real physiological variations between nights.
calculs.t0.movingWindow.label: Moving window
calculs.t0.movingWindow.pro1: Tracks slow sensor drift without amplifying night-to-night noise
calculs.t0.movingWindow.pro2: Automatically recovers missed nights via neighbouring nights
calculs.t0.movingWindow.ref: Granier 1985; Lu et al. 2004; Pasqualotto et al. 2019
calculs.t0.movingWindow.title: Moving window — rolling baseline (Granier / Lu / Pasqualotto)
calculs.t0.preDawn.con1: Fails when nighttime transpiration is non-negligible (hydraulic recharge, nighttime VPD, wind) — ΔT0ax overestimated
calculs.t0.preDawn.con2: No inter-day smoothing: a bad night yields a quirky T0 for that night (use Moving window to smooth)
calculs.t0.preDawn.desc: Mean of the N highest ΔT over the nocturnal window
calculs.t0.preDawn.how: For each night, keeps the N highest ΔT inside the configurable nocturnal window (Night start / Night end sliders), then averages them. The default 20h–8h spans the whole night; you can narrow it to pre-dawn (e.g. 4h–6h) for strict classic Granier. Assumption: during the nocturnal window, sap flow is zero (or minimal) so ΔT ≈ ΔT0ax.
calculs.t0.preDawn.label: Nocturnal max
calculs.t0.preDawn.pro1: Standard and simple — the reference baseline in TTD/Granier literature
calculs.t0.preDawn.pro2: Averaging the top N (rather than the single max) smooths spurious peaks and stays robust to noise
calculs.t0.preDawn.title: Nocturnal max — generalized Granier 1985
calculs.t0Helper: Method for determining T0 (= ΔT0ax, the reference value assumed at zero flow). Hover a tile to see how each method works.
calculs.t0steps.alphaNote: α (= {alpha}) is not used in this regression: it only serves the final sap flow Fd = α·K^β.
calculs.t0steps.s1.d: For each night, keep the daytime points (6h–20h) with a valid T600 and a matched ETo value (lookup second → hour → day).
calculs.t0steps.s2.d: Linearize the relation: X = ETo to the power 1/β, Y = inverse of T600.
calculs.t0steps.s3.d: Every diurnal point (6h–20h) with a valid T600 and a matched ETo feeds the regression. To narrow it down, set a manual hour or X range below.
calculs.t0steps.s3.d.manual: Keep only points whose hour and/or X fall within the manual ranges you set. If fewer than 5 pass, the regression is skipped for that night and T0 is left undefined.
calculs.t0steps.s4.d: Slope = median of the slopes over all point pairs; intercept = median of residuals. Insensitive to outliers.
calculs.t0steps.s4b.d: Keep only the points below the first line (Yᵢ ≤ slope·Xᵢ + intercept) — these are the days where flow is closest to zero — and refit Theil-Sen on them. The new intercept gives a T0 less biased by high-flow days. Skipped if fewer than 3 points pass.
calculs.t0steps.s5.d: The zero-flow reference is the inverse of the intercept. One value per night, timestamped at 20h.

docs.faq.q1.a: Yes — it means the model is worse than a constant mean. Usual causes: (1) uninformative predictors (e.g. a single sensor with no weather), (2) the sensor was disconnected in the training window, (3) the Fast preset is insufficient. Fixes: add VPD/PAR/Ta, change the model (Random Forest), widen the training window, check the targets chart.
docs.faq.q1.q: My R² is negative after training — is that bad?
docs.faq.q10.a: The 'Reset → raw' button at the top of Data Cleaning (right of the source bar). It clears the Cleaned dataset on the backend; the pipeline automatically falls back to raw_data. Your computed datasets (T600, Tslope, etc.) are preserved.
docs.faq.q10.q: How do I undo a cleaning run that broke everything?
docs.faq.q2.a: Path A = classical statistical methods (IQR, MAD, etc.). No training, instant. Path B = trains an ML model that predicts each sensor from the others + weather, then replaces outliers with the predictions. More powerful but needs richer data.
docs.faq.q2.q: What is the difference between Path A and Path B?
docs.faq.q3.a: Not mandatory — if the import quality banner is green (≥ 90% everywhere), you can go straight to Calculations. The pipeline runs on cleaned_data if present, otherwise on raw_data.
docs.faq.q3.q: Do you always need to clean data before running the TTD pipeline?
docs.faq.q4.a: NO. Otherwise the model learns to predict itself (perfect R² but useless). The app refuses training if you make this mistake (since the recent safeguard).
docs.faq.q4.q: Can targets and predictors contain the same columns?
docs.faq.q5.a: Because we haven't integrated candle yet (200 MB of deps + several days of dev). For now LSTM/BiLSTM/GRU go through a simple feed-forward MLP. The real LSTM will come later without an API break. For typical needs, Random Forest or SVR often do better.
docs.faq.q6.a: Save a Scenario (Scenarios tab) — it captures the full config (TTD method, params, cleaning method, predictors, metrics, seed=42 everywhere). Reloading the scenario restores the config; you retrain with one click and get exactly the same numbers.
docs.faq.q6.q: How do I reproduce the exact same analysis later?
docs.faq.q7.a: OK — the app matches by 'closest earlier value within 30 min'. If the gap exceeds 30 min, the value is NaN for that timestamp. If the time steps differ a lot (e.g. hourly weather vs 30-min sensors), consider resampling beforehand.
docs.faq.q7.q: My env file (VPD/PAR) does not align exactly to my sensors' timestamps
docs.faq.q8.a: k=3 by default (~3σ of a normal distribution, i.e. 99.7%). k=2 is more aggressive (catches more anomalies but more false positives). k=5 is conservative (only flags very large deviations). Calibrate according to the known data quality: reliable sensor → k=4-5, dubious sensor → k=2-3.
docs.faq.q8.q: What value to use for the k × RMSE threshold in gap filling?

docs.gloss.aicBic.def: Information criteria penalized by complexity. Smaller is better. Useful to compare several models.
docs.gloss.baseline.def: Nocturnal baseline with cyclic reset. Represents the theoretical zero-flow level.
docs.gloss.ctd.def: Continuous Thermal Dissipation (Granier 1985). Continuous heating, ΔT measured throughout the day. WARNING: this is NOT the method we use; it is the one in SapFlower / TREX / Baseliner.
docs.gloss.deltaT.def: Difference Tslope − Baseline. Represents the effect of heating.
docs.gloss.fd.def: Sap flow density in l·dm⁻²·h⁻¹. Formula: Fd = α × K^β. α and β are the calibration parameters (12.95 and 1 by default, Granier).
docs.gloss.gap.def: Hole in the data (missing value / NaN). Causes: outage, disconnection, battery.
docs.gloss.k.def: K = (ΔT0ax − ΔT) / ΔT. Normalized index, typically between 0 and 1.
docs.gloss.outlier.def: Value abnormally far from expected behavior. Causes: faulty sensor, datalogger gone wild, extreme event.
docs.gloss.par.def: Photosynthetically Active Radiation (µmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹). Light usable for photosynthesis.
docs.gloss.ptt.def: Predictor = model input. Target = column to predict/clean. Test = hold-out, never modified, only for evaluation.
docs.gloss.r2.def: Coefficient of determination. 1 = perfect, 0 = equivalent to a constant mean, negative = worse than a mean.
docs.gloss.rmse.def: Root Mean Square Error. Lower is better. RMSE/mean × 100% gives the error percentage.
docs.gloss.t600.def: Temperature measured 600 seconds (10 min) after the start of heating in a TTD cycle. Central signal of the analysis.
docs.gloss.tmax.def: Nocturnal maximum of ΔT, assumed to correspond to zero sap flow. 4 methods to compute it (Nocturnal max, Moving window, Double regression, Env data / VpdPar).
docs.gloss.tslope.def: Temperature slope over the 30-min window — first step of the pipeline.
docs.gloss.ttd.def: Transient Thermal Dissipation (Do & Rocheteau 2002). Cyclic heating method, 15min ON / 15min OFF. The relevant signal is T600. This is what TTDprocess implements.
docs.gloss.ttdPlus.def: Harmonic evolution of TTD (De Sousa & Do 2025). Fourier analysis of the heating cycle to extract amplitude α and phase φ.
docs.gloss.vpd.def: Vapor Pressure Deficit. Indicator of the atmosphere's evaporative potential (kPa). Major driver of transpiration.
docs.gloss.vpdPar.def: Robust method to identify ΔT0ax: cumulative conditions (night + low PAR + low VPD + thermal stability).

docs.t0etp.overviewP1: The "Diurnal regression" method estimates the zero-flow reference ΔT0ax (called T0) from potential evapotranspiration (ETo), without assuming zero night-time flow. It follows Regaldo & Ritter (2007, Tree Physiology) and is useful when nocturnal transpiration or hydraulic recharge make Granier's nocturnal-zero-flow assumption unreliable.
docs.t0etp.overviewP2: On diurnal points (6h–20h), it fits  1/T600 = slope · ETo^(1/β) + intercept  by robust regression (Theil-Sen). The reference is then  T0 = 1 / intercept.
docs.t0etp.s1.check: The daytime points kept, with valid ETo and T600 (> 0).
docs.t0etp.s2.check: The move from raw measurements to the regression variables.
docs.t0etp.s3.check: The points kept within the tolerance band around the mean X̄ (column "retenu").
docs.t0etp.s4.check: The slope, intercept and r² of the robust fit.
docs.t0etp.s4.formula: Theil-Sen: slope = median of slopes ; intercept = median(Y − slope·X)
docs.t0etp.s5.check: The final T0 value (column "T0 (=1/ordonnee)"), used as-is in the tm table. Nights with no T0 (regression skipped) appear empty in the tm table.
docs.t0etp.stepsTip: After running the pipeline with the "Diurnal regression" method, these 5 tables appear in the Table tab (T0 ① to ⑤). Every row can be recomputed by hand, and each table is exportable from the Export tab.
docs.t0etp.verifyBody: To cross-check: in table ⑤, the "T0 (=1/ordonnee)" value of a sensor T600_X on a given date must equal column "T0_X" in the t0 table (the 20:00 row of that night). β is the same exponent used in the sap flow Fd = α·K^β (set in Settings).
docs.voieA.m1.idea: Rejects any value outside a physical [min, max] range. Mandatory first step (negative temperatures, astronomical values).
docs.voieA.m1.name: Absolute bounds
docs.voieA.m1.use: Always enabled at the start of a classical pipeline.
docs.voieA.m2.idea: Q1 - k·IQR ≤ x ≤ Q3 + k·IQR with k=1.5 (Tukey). Standard statistical method.
docs.voieA.m2.name: IQR — Interquartile Range
docs.voieA.m2.use: Quick first pass, robust to most distributions. Start here.
docs.voieA.m3.idea: |x - μ|/σ > threshold (typically 3). Assumes a Gaussian distribution.
docs.voieA.m3.name: Z-Score
docs.voieA.m3.use: When data is approximately normal (Gaussian noise). Otherwise prefer MAD.
docs.voieA.m4.idea: Robust Z-Score variant: uses median + MAD instead of mean + standard deviation. Insensitive to up to 50% outliers.
docs.voieA.m4.name: MAD — Median Absolute Deviation
docs.voieA.m4.use: Recommended default on sensor data. The most reliable of the 3 statistical methods.
docs.voieA.m5.idea: Computes σ over sliding windows. Too-high σ = excessive noise. Too-low σ = sensor stuck or disconnected.
docs.voieA.m5.name: Rolling Window
docs.voieA.m5.use: Detects time-localized failures that no global outlier filter would catch.
docs.voieA.m6.idea: Compares the daily max to the N neighbors. If max < ratio × neighbor_max, the day is flipped (datalogger gone wild).
docs.voieA.m6.name: Reverse Detection
docs.voieA.m6.use: Detects days where day/night were swapped. Common on fragile solar-powered systems.
docs.voieA.m7.idea: 100 random trees isolate points. Anomaly score = ease of isolation. Natively multivariate.
docs.voieA.m7.name: Isolation Forest
docs.voieA.m7.use: When outliers involve several columns at once (e.g. SF1 high + SF2 low).
docs.voieA.overviewP1g: : each method is an explicit formula, no trained model. Advantage: fast (a few seconds), no weather data required. Drawback: it ignores physical context (a midday spike with VPD=3 kPa is legitimate, the same spike at night is anomalous — Path A cannot tell the difference).
docs.voieA.overviewP2: Workflow: pick a method, target columns, a replacement strategy (NaN / linear interpolation / forward-fill / moving average), and run. Result: a Cleaned dataset with outliers replaced.
docs.voieA.tipA: Tip: in the Data Cleaning tab, click the
docs.voieA.tipB: next to each method for the full documentation (parameters, limits, references).
docs.voieB.choose1b: : Multiple Linear with the Standard preset. Gives a baseline to beat.
docs.voieB.choose2b: : switch to Random Forest (the most versatile).
docs.voieB.choose4a: If you want to quantify uncertainty
docs.voieB.choose5a: If there is strong temporal dependence
docs.voieB.choose5b: (e.g. VPD of the last few hours): ARX / ARMAX.
docs.voieB.choose6b: : v1 = MLP for now. Often produces results close to a Random Forest.
docs.voieB.m1.how: y = a·x + b on 1 predictor. Reference (baseline).
docs.voieB.m1.name: Simple Linear
docs.voieB.m2.how: y = β₀ + β₁·x₁ + ... + βₙ·xₙ on n predictors.
docs.voieB.m2.name: Multiple Linear
docs.voieB.m3.how: Ensemble of N bootstrapped regression trees. Captures non-linearities.
docs.voieB.m3.name: Random Forest
docs.voieB.m4.how: ε tolerance margin with RBF kernel by default.
docs.voieB.m4.name: SVR (Support Vector Regression)
docs.voieB.m5.how: Bayesian, also yields a confidence interval.
docs.voieB.m5.name: GPR (Gaussian Process)
docs.voieB.m6.how: Regression on lagged predictors. ARMAX = ARX + MA smoothing.
docs.voieB.m6.name: ARX / ARMAX
docs.voieB.m6.pros: Captures the temporal dependence on exogenous variables.
docs.voieB.m7.cons: v1 = MLP, not a true sequential LSTM.
docs.voieB.m7.how: v1 = 1-hidden-layer feed-forward MLP (until candle integration ships).
docs.voieB.m7.name: LSTM / BiLSTM / GRU
docs.voieB.m7.pros: Able to learn complex patterns with time features.
docs.voieB.overviewP1c: learns the expected behavior of each sensor from other variables (other sensors, weather, hour, day of year). It predicts the "normal" value for each timestamp, compares it to the observation, and flags/replaces values that deviate too far.
docs.voieB.overviewP2b: : it takes context into account. A spike at 2pm with VPD=3 kPa is legitimate, the same spike at night with VPD=0.05 kPa is anomalous — regardless of its absolute value.
